title: The Levi-Civita connection and Christoffel symbols
summary: Why vector fields have no canonical derivative; the directional derivative on Euclidean space and its five properties; connections on vector bundles, torsion and metric compatibility; the Koszul formula, uniqueness and the fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry; Christoffel symbols, their formula, symmetry and non-tensorial transformation, with the polar-coordinate example; the tangential connection and second fundamental form of a submanifold.

objectives.description: Define connections, torsion and metric compatibility, derive the Koszul formula and prove existence and uniqueness of the Levi-Civita connection.
Compute Christoffel symbols from the metric coefficients, with the index conventions stated, and check torsion-freeness and metric compatibility on an example.
Explain why Christoffel symbols are not tensor components and read coordinate blow-ups (cot θ at the poles, 1/r at the origin) as coordinate artefacts.
Prove that the tangential projection of the ambient Levi-Civita connection is the Levi-Civita connection of a submanifold and compute it for the round sphere.

preparation.description: Read Gudmundsson chapter 6, pp. 77–78: the directional derivative and Proposition 6.1; Definition 6.2 (connection) and Definition 6.3 (torsion).
Read p. 79: Definition 6.4 (metric connection), Observation 6.5 (Koszul formula) and Definition 6.6; then pp. 80–81: Remark 6.7, Proposition 6.8 and Theorem 6.9 with their proofs.
Read pp. 82–83: Proposition 6.12 (Lie groups) and Example 6.13 (Christoffel symbols and their formula).
Read pp. 84–86: Definitions 6.14–6.19 (extensions, tangential and normal parts, second fundamental form), Theorem 6.20, Proposition 6.21, Example 6.23.
Open-licensed alternative reading: Sternberg chapter 3, §3.1 (linear connections) and §3.2 (Christoffel symbols), and §3.9 (Levi-Civita's theorem); Wendl §1.1 for the motivation.

activities.title: Chapter 6 with the lesson: connections and the Koszul formula
activities.instructions: Read the lesson alongside Gudmundsson chapter 6. After Observation 6.5, close the notes and re-derive the Koszul formula yourself from the two conditions before reading on. Recompute the polar-coordinate Christoffel symbols by hand.

activities.title: Tutorial: Christoffel symbols of the sphere; the tangential connection
activities.instructions: Attempt exercise 1 first, stating the index convention before computing; show the work for every non-zero symbol and check one metric-compatibility identity. Then attempt exercise 2, organising the proof around the fundamental theorem. Submit each attempt when complete; revise after feedback.

activities.title: Explain: what torsion-free and metric each buy
activities.instructions: Exercise 3, written without the notes, then compared with Theorem 6.9 and its proof.

activities.title: Retrieval: definitions and formulas
activities.instructions: From memory: the three axioms of a connection; torsion; metric compatibility; the Koszul formula; the Christoffel formula with index placement; the statement of Theorem 6.20.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: inverse metric computed; Γ^θ_φφ = −sinθ cosθ and Γ^φ_θφ = Γ^φ_φθ = cotθ derived with all other symbols shown to vanish; one metric-compatibility identity checked; the blow-up of cotθ at the poles explained as a coordinate artefact; independence of R proved.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Christoffel symbols are the components of a tensor, so if they vanish at a point in one chart they vanish in every chart.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Their transformation law has an inhomogeneous second-derivative term. Normal coordinates make them vanish at a point; polar coordinates on the flat plane make them non-zero everywhere.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Γ^φ_θφ = cotθ blows up at the poles, so the Levi-Civita connection of the sphere is singular there.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The connection is the tangential projection of the Euclidean directional derivative (Theorem 6.20), manifestly smooth on the whole sphere; the blow-up reflects the degeneration of the spherical chart, as in unit 1.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Metric compatibility alone determines the connection.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Adding to a metric connection any tensor A with g(A(X,Y),Z) antisymmetric in (Y,Z) gives another metric connection; torsion-freeness is what removes the freedom. Exercise 3 asks for examples.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The directional derivative of a tangent field along a surface in R³ is tangent to the surface.
commonMisconceptions.correction: In general it has a normal component, the second fundamental form B(X,Y); only its tangential part is the surface's covariant derivative. For the sphere of radius R, B(X,Y) = −R^{-2}⟨X,Y⟩p is never zero for X = Y ≠ 0.

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Build agent re-derived: the Koszul formula from the three permuted compatibility identities; polar symbols Γ^r_θθ = −r, Γ^θ_rθ = 1/r checked against the Cartesian directional derivative; sphere symbols from g = R²(dθ² + sin²θ dφ²): g^θθ = R^{-2}, g^φφ = (R² sin²θ)^{-1}, Γ^θ_φφ = −sinθ cosθ, Γ^φ_θφ = cotθ, others zero, with ∂_θ g_φφ = 2 g(∇_∂θ ∂φ, ∂φ) = 2R² sinθ cosθ verified; independence of R from the Koszul formula; tangential connection: C^∞-linearity and Leibniz via linearity of ⊤, torsion-freeness via tangency of brackets of tangent fields (slice-chart argument), metric compatibility via h(∇_X Y, Z) = h((∇_X Y)^⊤, Z) for Z tangent; sphere: ⟨∂_X Y, p⟩ = −⟨X, Y⟩ hence ∇̃_X Y = ∂_X Y + R^{-2}⟨X,Y⟩p and B(X,Y) = −R^{-2}⟨X,Y⟩p; the examples ∂ + X × Y (metric, torsion) and ∂ + X(f)Y + Y(f)X (torsion-free, not metric).
